description: We are a two person interdisciplinary engineering and computer science duo from Indonesia: Kiran Kumar specializing in biomedical digital signal processing and ECG feature engineering, and Dion Pasaribu specializing in machine learning architectures and interactive web deployment. Combining signal processing physics with ensemble AI, we build reliable, low-latency health monitoring software for space exploration. (Note: Our team roster is complete and closed with our two core members.)
summary: We develops an autonomous, edge ready 12-lead ECG health monitoring system designed for astronauts on long-duration space missions. Instead of relying on a single one-size-fits-all model, our system uses a specialized 6-head architecture that pairs each cardiac diagnostic task (Rhythm, PVC, PAC, BBB, AV Block, and ST Elevation) with its optimal digital filter (IIR Butterworth, FIR Blackman, or IIR Chebyshev Type II) and tree-based ML model (XGBoost, LightGBM, or Random Forest). Trained on multi source clinical ECG repositories and contextualized with NASA spaceflight cardiovascular data, our lightweight web platform delivers fast, explainable arrhythmia screening without depending on Earth to space communication latency
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

OrbitalECGBeats is a browser-based 12-lead ECG screening tool built to monitor astronaut heart health during long-duration space missions. When given a raw 12-lead ECG recording, the system first cleans baseline drift and high-frequency electrical noise using zero-phase digital bandpass filtering (0.05–40 Hz with odd-reflection edge padding). It then extracts 14 physiological features from each of the 12 leads covering signal amplitude statistics, R-peak counts, heart rate variability (SDNN and RMSSD), and QRS complex duration resulting in 168 lead-specific features per recording, which are contextualized against a Spaceflight Microgravity & HRV Baseline (NASA OSDR Reference) to account for autonomic shifts in orbit. Instead of sending all recordings through a single generic model, OrbitalECGBeats routes the extracted features through six specialized diagnostic heads, each compressed to its top 8 features via Sequential Feature Selection (SFS) to screen for Cardiac Rhythm abnormalities, Premature Ventricular Contractions (PVC), Premature Atrial Contractions (PAC), Bundle Branch Block (BBB), Atrioventricular (AV) Block, and ST Elevation within seconds.

What benefits does it have?

By pairing lightweight tabular tree models with targeted digital filtering, OrbitalECGBeats runs fast on low-power onboard hardware without needing cloud connectivity or continuous Earth to space data links. Unlike black box deep neural networks that require heavy GPU compute and offer little clinical transparency, our feature based pipeline lets crew medical officers see exactly which lead metrics and waveform changes triggered an alert. It also includes built in signal quality gating requiring at least two valid beats, at least 50% valid R-peaks, and QRS durations between 40 and 200 ms before accepting a measurement so noisy leads from astronaut movement are flagged as missing rather than producing false alarms.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Spaceflight exposes astronauts to prolonged microgravity, fluid shifts, and cosmic radiation that can alter cardiac electrophysiology and trigger arrhythmias far from hospital care. OrbitalECGBeats is designed to give deep-space crews an autonomous early-warning system capable of catching subtle conduction blocks, ectopic beats, or ischemic ST changes before they escalate into mission-critical emergencies. Beyond space exploration, the same lightweight architecture can run on standard laptops or portable clinic setups on Earth, helping rural healthcare workers perform reliable 12-lead ECG triage in remote areas where specialist cardiologists are unavailable.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

We built the machine learning and signal processing pipeline in Python using WFDB for reading ECG records, NumPy and SciPy for digital filtering (IIR Butterworth, Blackman FIR, and IIR Chebyshev Type II), waveform feature extraction, and patient-level data splitting, alongside scikit-learn, XGBoost, Random Forrest, and LightGBM for model training, PyYAML for experiment configuration, Matplotlib for signal visualization, and Joblib for model serialization. Model training and validation combined three public PhysioNet 12-lead ECG repositories Chapman-Shaoxing (500 Hz), PTB-XL (500 Hz), and Leipzig Heart Center (977 Hz) paired with a Spaceflight Microgravity and HRV Baseline (NASA OSDR Reference) for orbital cardiovascular context. For the web application, we developed a TypeScript and React frontend built with Vite and styled with Tailwind CSS, incorporating local Shadcn-style UI components (class-variance-authority and tailwind-merge), React Router, and Lucide icons, paired with a Python backend running FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn, and Joblib to serve model predictions. Regarding hardware, no dedicated physical ECG sensor or flight-qualified spacecraft hardware is integrated or validated, local edge AI inference is framed as a deployment concept, and the platform runs on standard computers where users can test uploaded ECG signals, extracted feature files, or built in samples from the training dataset.

How is your project creative?

Most automated ECG classifiers apply one uniform filter and one model to every cardiac condition, which creates a trade-off: heavy smoothing removes noise but can flatten subtle wave features needed for certain diagnoses, while light filtering preserves morphology at the cost of extra artifact. Our creative leap is treating signal preprocessing and model selection as a coupled, task-specific routing problem across six independent heads. Rather than forcing a single pipeline to compromise, each head uses the exact filter-and-model pair proven strongest for that specific pathology: FIR Blackman (501 taps) paired with LightGBM for Cardiac Rhythm (86.93% Macro-F1) and PAC (63.29% Macro-F1); FIR Blackman paired with Random Forest for BBB (92.26% Macro-F1) and ST Elevation (85.76% Macro-F1); IIR Chebyshev Type II (Order 4, 74 dB stopband) paired with Random Forest for PVC (61.24% Macro-F1); and IIR Butterworth Zero-Phase (Order 4) paired with XGBoost for AV Block (50.91% Macro-F1).

What factors did your team consider?

We focused on three practical constraints : preventing data leakage across patients, handling noisy leads safely, and validating imbalanced classes under realistic compute limits. First, we split all multi-source datasets strictly by patient ID so recordings from the same person never leaked between training and evaluation sets. Second, when compressing our 168 extracted features down to 8 features per head using Sequential Feature Selection (SFS), we deliberately chose 2 fold cross-validation (K = 2) for two reasons. Because SFS evaluates hundreds of feature subsets iteratively from 168 down to 8, using a larger K would multiply training time without improving feature stability. More importantly, several diagnostic heads such as PVC and higher-grade AV blocks contain very few positive cases; splitting those rare samples across 5 or 10 folds would fragment the minority classes too thinly, whereas K = 2 ensures every fold retains as complete a set of classes as possible during training and validation.
